book: 019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!

chapters.file: ch03 - Popular Culture and Philosophy™ Series Editor William Irwin.md
ch06 - And Where the @#$%^& is the Queen.md
chapters.relation: The editors' introduction recounts Monty Python's 1969 debut and argues the troupe's absurdism bears a deep connection to philosophy because the British Pythons absorbed the Oxford and Cambridge linguistic analysis of Russell, Wittgenstein, Moore, and Ryle while at university in the 1960s. It tours the volume's three parts, previewing each contributor's pairing: Schilbrack reading Life of Brian through Camus's absurd hero, Brighouse using the Argument Clinic for Rawls's analysis of social practices, Asma finding Buddhist mindfulness in The Meaning of Life, Huss pairing the Pythons with Hume on religion, and Spinelli reading sketches through Foucault on the social construction of madness. It concludes there is no single connection between Python and philosophy but many: sketches illuminate philosophy, philosophy illuminates sketches, and Python's empire says something about philosophy's cultural standing (with Wittgenstein's duck-rabbit figuring how the remaining chapters can be seen).

chapters.file: ch07 - Philosophical Aspects of Monty Python.md
ch08 - “Life’s a Piece of Shit” The Question of Heroism.md
chapters.relation: Argues Life of Brian is heretical rather than blasphemous: it never mocks Jesus or belief in God but ridicules gullible, smug believing — the Sermon on the Mount crowd mishearing 'blessed are the cheesemakers,' the sandal schism — a critique the chapter aligns with Hume on the appetite for the marvelous and on anthropomorphism. It reads Brian's window sermon ('You're all individuals... think for yourselves') as Kant's Sapere aude and as an existentialist, possibly Christian, humanism. Against the charge of nihilism, it places Brian squarely in Camus's absurd universe (the pointless crucifixion finale and 'Always Look on the Bright Side of Life') and asks whether Brian is an absurd hero like Sisyphus, Meursault, or Dr. Rieux; he is not — he never scorns his fate — so the chapter proposes 'absurd decent guy': Brian lives sincerely, without waiting for miracles, and humor rather than revolt is the counterweight to absurdity.

Asks how the exploding-glutton Mr. Creosote sequence in 'The Autumn Years' of The Meaning of Life can provoke laughter rather than horror, given that Creosote shares the monster's marks of physiological impossibility and disgusting category-violation (like Frankenstein's monster or the Alien). The answer: horror requires disgust plus fear, and Creosote, like the slapstick clown, is marked as neither able to harm nor be harmed, so the audience's fear-condition for horror is never met. A second layer of the laughter is vindictive: the maitre d''s wafer-thin mint is retributive justice, a morality-play punishment for gluttony in the lineage of Spenser's Gluttony and Dante's Inferno, so black comedy trades on our sense that the victim deserves what he gets.

Uses 'Piston Engine (a Bargain)' from the Hamlet episode of Flying Circus — park-bench women who buy gift-wrapped piston engines because 'it was a bargain,' kill birds with hurled groceries, and end by dazedly reciting Hamlet — to test Wittgenstein's theories of meaning. Both the early Verification Principle and the later meaning-as-use principle fail: we understand the meaning of every sentence yet cannot make sense of what the women are saying, just as 'This is my hand' at the doctor's office, or the philosopher's 'I know that that's a tree' (Wittgenstein's joke at Moore's expense), is meaningful but senseless in context. Drawing on Remarks on Colour and On Certainty, Smith concludes that communal practices and forms of life fix what it makes sense to say, and that the sketch proves Python's Horatio point — 'there are more things in heaven and earth than are dreamt of in your philosophy' — since no theory of meaning captures what makes the exchange funny.

chapters.file: ch11 - Suppose You Were Attached to a Dead Parrot The Role of Thought Experiments.md
chapters.relation: Takes the Argument Clinic sketch — Mr. Vibrating's pure contradiction versus the customer's demand for 'a connected series of statements intended to establish a proposition' — to argue that paying for good argument is not absurd, because only sustained argument with others gets most of us true beliefs about complex matters. It explains Rawls's method of reflective equilibrium (testing general principles against considered judgments about cases, illustrated by the author's Rimbaud/Rambo censorship blunder) and Judith Jarvis Thomson's violinist thought experiment, showing how such experiments force us to abandon groundless reasons: opponents of abortion who let the violinist go must find grounds other than the fetus's right to life. Good thought experiments, it closes, work like good Python sketches — the Dead Parrot sketch's internally logical absurdity — so a real argument clinic would serve a genuine social function, since interlocutors expose biases that solitary reflection cannot.

chapters.file: ch12 - Getting Right with Brian (Just in Case).md
chapters.relation: Reads Life of Brian through Nietzsche's madman: the crowd's laughter at Brian's market sermons ('consider the lilies... have the birds got jobs?') enacts the death of the cheerless, pathos-soaked God, with Brian as a sincere 'divine idiot' who escapes ressentiment by falling idiotically below the dialectic rather than rising above it as an Übermensch. Bergson's account of the comic — rigidity invisible to its bearer, 'as though wearing the ring of Gyges with reverse effect' — explains why the Pythons' straight men, British class consciousness, and the Roman/British empires ('Romani ite domum,' the centurion's Latin lesson) are funny, and why Britons and Romans can laugh at themselves while Americans cannot. Pivoting from Jorge's war on laughter in Eco's The Name of the Rose, the chapter closes with a Pascal's-wager parody: having laughed at Brian, you have already wagered your immortal soul on God being British — the sort of God who can take a joke.

chapters.file: ch13 - Yes, but What About the Killer Rabbit.md
chapters.relation: Argues the Pythons invert Arthurian legend's traditional patriarchal function, using Holy Grail — made amid 1970s women's liberation and legal abortion — to expose the absurdity of patriarchy rather than endorse it. The Black Knight's 'None shall pass' embodies an abstract, relationship-blind masculine ethics that the chapter sets against care ethics, while the witch-weighing scene shows Arthur and Bedevere's male bonding eclipsing the mob's victim. Castle Anthrax's 'perilous bed' and the Prince Herbert rescue — Launcelot's heterosexual-matrix heroics collapsing when the damsel in the tower is a prince who enjoys musicals — turn courtly love and gender roles into farce, making the film as much a document of 1970s gender politics as a medieval satire.

Reads The Meaning of Life as a sustained reductio of transcendentalism — the two-world metaphysics shared by Plato, Augustine, and Vedanta's Brahman/atman — arguing that the film's dehumanizing sketches (the machine that goes 'ping,' the 'every sperm is sacred' father selling his children, the Vegas-style Christmas in Heaven) show how otherworldly belief overrides this-worldly compassion. It parallels the Buddha's scriptural critiques: the Agganna sutta against caste, the no-self (anatta) doctrine against the Bhagavad Gita's soul that licenses Krishna to tell Arjuna killing is a favor, and impermanence (anicca) against the fantasy of eternal bliss. Python's grotesque — Creosote's explosion, the organ-donor lady's 'Galaxy Song' despair — matches Buddhist corpse meditations, while the film steers between hedonism (Creosote) and nihilism (the housewife who surrenders her liver) toward the Buddha's Middle Way and, against everyday distraction (the boardroom's 'people are not wearing enough hats,' the couple who think Schopenhauer begins with an S), toward mindfulness (sati).

chapters.file: ch15 - And Now for . . . Comedic Eliminativism.md
chapters.relation: Argues The Meaning of Life dismantles the 'axial' picture of life as a journey toward a salvific destination (Jaspers's Axial Age thinking), instanced in the headmaster who announces Jenkins's mother's death between Empire Day announcements, the tank fish who never connect Howard's being eaten to their own fate, and the restaurant couple ordering 'philosophy for two' with no appetite for wisdom. The classical answers all fail as delivered: Socrates's philosophy as learning how to die, Heidegger's claim that facing death reveals one's own unique possibilities, and Kant's three questions (What can I know? What should I do? For what may I hope?) collapse into the question of life's meaning, but religion has gone stale and philosophy has become detached trivia. The Pythons instead accomplish the user-friendly domestication of the death of God — the hearty laughter Nietzsche and Derrida counsel — and the chapter coins 'comedic eliminativism' on the model of eliminative materialism's dissolution of Descartes's mind-body problem: replace the yearning for the meaning of life with altered reactions, laughter itself as the solution to the riddle.

chapters.file: ch17 - Prayer (A Euphemism for Butt-Kissing and Begging).md
chapters.relation: Argues the Pythons' religious gags perform philosophy's preliminary job of challenging doctrine: the 'every sperm is sacred' family makes God a voyeur of contraception, the Life of Brian stoning (rocks flying each time anyone utters 'Jehovah') shows blasphemy law run absurd, and 'Christmas in Heaven' exposes heavenly reward as material compensation. Deploying Socrates and Plato — the Republic's ban on portraying pettiful gods, the Apology on why the virtuous need not fear death, and above all the Euthyphro — the chapter reads the witch-weighing and the Holy Hand Grenade as the ancient problem whether acts are just because God sanctions them, and the chaplain's toadying prayer against God's own 'don't grovel' as proof that sacrifice and prayer are bargaining a perfect being has no need of. The upshot is not atheism but the Socratic verdict that the mobs punishing blasphemy, not the mocked, are the real blasphemers.

chapters.file: ch18 - The Epilogue A Question of Belief.md
chapters.relation: Systematically pairs Hume's philosophy of religion with Python parodies: Anselm's ontological argument fails because existence cannot be defined into a concept (the Yeti-spotter who never spotted one), with Arthur 'Two Sheds' Jackson, Ron Obvious, and Confuse-A-Cat illustrating the gap between conceivability and possibility; the Galaxy Song's cosmic order and the mock hymn 'All Things Dull and Ugly' stage the design argument and Hume's reply that creation shows moral indifference as readily as benevolence; and Brian's 'miracles' — being 'taken up' then spotted sprinting, curing Simon the hermit by landing on his foot — illustrate Hume's 'Of Miracles' on the unreliability of testimony. Hume's Natural History claim that the cause of religion is fear surfaces in the 'O Father, please don't boil us' hymn and in Arthur's groveling before a God who hates it. Both Hume and the Pythons end in suspended judgment about God — settled, if at all, only by the wrestling match in which 'God exists by two falls to a submission.'

holes.name: Incongruity Theory of Humor (comic vs horrific)
holes.what: The theory that comic amusement arises from perceived incongruity or category-violation, with Carroll's addition that horror requires disgust plus fear, so non-threatening violation yields laughter.
holes.why: Chapter 9's whole account of why Mr. Creosote's explosion is funny rather than horrific is built on this theory, and the taxonomy's only humor slug (bergson-laughter) is Bergson's specific theory, which the chapter never uses.

holes.name: Reflective Equilibrium
holes.what: Rawls's method of testing general moral principles against considered judgments about particular cases and adjusting each against the other, ideally in conversation with others, until they cohere.
holes.why: Chapter 11 argues the Argument Clinic sketch shows why this method — not mere contradiction — is how philosophical argument justifies moral beliefs, and no existing Rawls slug (veil of ignorance, justice as fairness) covers it.

holes.name: Mindfulness (sati)
holes.what: The Buddhist discipline of focused, present-moment meditative awareness that cuts through distraction and craving.
holes.why: Chapter 14's title and conclusion ('Mind the Mindfulness') identify mindfulness as the positive alternative the film and the Buddha both offer to transcendentalism and distraction; the taxonomy has only Zen, not sati.

holes.name: Karl Jaspers
holes.what: German existential philosopher who coined the 'Axial Age' (Achsenzeit), construing the last 2,500 years as the working-out of the world-religions' picture of life as a journey to transcendence.
holes.why: Chapter 15 builds its entire critique of The Meaning of Life around Jaspers's notion of 'axial' thinking — life as a journey to a destination — which Python's comedy supposedly reduces to absurdity, and no taxonomy entry covers him or the axial-age concept.
